[00:00:00] Naomi Patel: Alright everyone, thanks for joining. This is Naomi from Redwood, I have Ethan with me, our SE. We're hoping to run through a methodology so when we do the benchmark runs in your VPC it's apples-to-apples. Um, quick intro?
[00:00:22] Maya Thompson: Hi, Maya - CTO at Arcadia. Thanks, yeah we want a reproducible methodology, and to understand tradeoffs for Dedicated vs private. Our key thing is latency for interactive clinician workflows.
[00:00:32] Ethan Liu: Hey, hi all. I'll lead the technical bits. Goal for today: align on prompt sets, load generator, how to measure warm vs cold KV cache, batching, and quantization checks.
[00:00:47] Ravi Singh: Sounds good. Quick note - our prompts vary between 20 tokens up to 800 tokens, median around 120 tokens. We'll share a sample set.
[00:00:55] Naomi Patel: Perfect, that's helpful. Ok let's start with the dataset. For apples-to-apples we recommend: a) representative sample of your real requests, b) explicit token length distribution, c) seed the PRNG so runs are repeatable. Ethan, walk through harness.
[00:01:12] Ethan Liu: Yeah so our harness is two parts: a load-generator that simulates clients with configurable concurrency and arrival distributions, and a runner that calls the Redwood endpoint (hosted or private) and records per-request timing including gateway time, model time, and token emit time. We instrument p50/p95/p99. Important: keep the prompt bodies identical across runs and include the exact model version string.
[00:01:37] Lena Ortiz: When you say "gateway time" do you mean ingress from our VPC to Redwood? We need to make sure network hops are measured.
[00:01:44] Ethan Liu: Yes, we capture client-to-gateway RTT, gateway-to-inference runtime, and end-to-end. For VPC runs we can deploy the runner inside your VPC so client->runner latency is minimal, leaving only the network hops we want to measure.
[00:02:02] Maya Thompson: Can we also instrument GPU metrics? We want utilization and memory to check batching behavior.
[00:02:08] Ethan Liu: Absolutely, we collect GPU utilization, NVLink stats where available, and kernel-level metrics if you consent. For Dedicated runs we expose those metrics, for Hosted we provide aggregated metrics.
[00:02:20] Naomi Patel: Ok next piece: KV cache warm vs cold. Typically we see huge p99 differences if you hit a model with an empty cache. We should define priming steps.
[00:02:31] Ravi Singh: Right, in our prod traffic there's a lot of repeated prefixes. How do you recommend measuring warm cache?
[00:02:36] Ethan Liu: Two runs: cold-start run where each prompt is first-seen (we flush caches between requests), then warm-run where we prime the KV cache by replaying a warm-up sequence that reflects the same prefix distribution. We'll capture per-token latency to show the difference. Also track key hit rates.
[00:02:55] Maya Thompson: How long should priming be? Do we do full corpus or a few hundred requests?
[00:03:01] Ethan Liu: We typically recommend priming until metric stabilization - that's often ~500-1,000 requests depending on your hit distribution. We'll look at hit-rate curve. We can automate detection of steady-state.
[00:03:12] Naomi Patel: Important to note: batching changes too. If you batch at request-time you'll save GPU cycles but may add latency. We need experiments that sweep batching sizes and observe p99 and per-token cost.
[00:03:26] Ravi Singh: Our SLA is interactive, p99 under 220ms for short prompts, so large batching may violate SLAs. But if we can batch only certain routes maybe ok.
[00:03:36] Ethan Liu: Exactly. We'll run parametric tests: 1) no batching (single-request), 2) small batching window (20ms), 3) larger window (50-100ms), and measure latency distribution and tokens/sec. We'll provide cost modeling—tokens per GPU-second—so you can see tradeoffs.
[00:03:52] Maya Thompson: Quantization - we use int8 on some workloads. How do you validate quality regressions?
[00:03:58] Ethan Liu: Two-part: qualitative and automated. Qualitative: a small evaluation set of representative prompts that you mark as high-sensitivity; we run both full-precision and quantized variants and do diff outputs and BLEU/ROUGE or task-specific metrics. Automated: embedding drift tests and log-likelihood deltas. We'll flag failure thresholds.
[00:04:21] Naomi Patel: Also note that certain kernels behave differently on different GPUs—so apples-to-apples means same model file/quantization and same runtime kernel selection when possible. We'll document the exact commit/version used.
[00:04:33] Lena Ortiz: On VPC/on-prem, network egress rates and path variance matter. For private runs, do you recommend we run Redwood's agent inside our cluster?
[00:04:42] Ethan Liu: For VPC private deployments we can run the agent in your VPC so inference happens in your environment. For on-prem, we'll instrument with a local runner. For both we ask for SSH or API keys to access metrics endpoints. We provide scripts to collect jstats, kernel traces, and kernel selection logs.
[00:04:57] Ravi Singh: What about variance from autoscaling? If we get spikes and nodes spin up, tails can increase.
[00:05:03] Ethan Liu: Good call. We'll lock down capacity for the benchmark, or run with controlled autoscaling but log scaling events. Ideally for a baseline you reserve capacity so you measure runtime characteristics without autoscale noise. We can run both modes.
[00:05:17] Naomi Patel: Let's talk about load generator specifics. Use Poisson arrivals? Constant-concurrency? Both?
[00:05:23] Ethan Liu: Both. Poisson is good for realistic arrival patterns. Constant concurrency is good for stress-testing throughput limits. We'll run: ramp-up, steady-state for 10-15 minutes, ramp-down. Also collect seed so run is reproducible.
[00:05:37] Maya Thompson: Is 10-15 minutes long enough to warm caches and measure steady-state?
[00:05:41] Ethan Liu: Depends on cache priming and corpus size. For our typical runs we do a warm-up of 15 minutes then a 30-minute steady-state, but we can shorten if you need. For initial POC we can do shorter: 5 minutes warm-up + 15 minutes steady-state.
[00:05:55] Naomi Patel: For apples-to-apples across model variants, lock tokenizer, same sampling/hot-start seeds, same model version. Also capture model size, quantization config, and kernel versions in metadata.
[00:06:11] Ravi Singh: How do we handle streaming responses and token-emission latency in metrics? We care about first-token latency as well as complete response time.
[00:06:18] Ethan Liu: We capture first-token time, last-token time, per-token inter-arrival times. First-token latency is critical for interactive flows. We'll provide both distributions.
[00:06:28] Maya Thompson: Security/compliance - you'll need access to our VPC. What sort of artifacts do you need? We've already looked at your security deck.
[00:06:34] Naomi Patel: We'll need a service account with minimal scope, dedicated test infra, and temporary keys. We'll use our ephemeral runner and delete after test. We can do network peering and only allow specific IP ranges. We'll also provide an architecture diagram in the repo.
[00:06:47] Lena Ortiz: Fine. We'll set up a build user and allow the runner to access metrics endpoints. We'll also want to ensure logs don't contain PHI. Is there an option to mask PII?
[00:06:55] Ethan Liu: Yes - our harness can hash or token-mask sensitive fields before logging. We can also run purely synthetic prompts derived from your distribution if you prefer no real data leaves the VPC.
[00:07:06] Naomi Patel: Ok moving on - comparing Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Key differences to call out: network egress and hop latency, kernel optimization availability, and how caching layers are shared or isolated.
[00:07:18] Ethan Liu: On Hosted, KV cache is shared at the node-level across tenants but segregated by customer. On Dedicated, you get dedicated workers so cache behavior may be more stable for your traffic. On Private, you control everything. So run design should test each scenario with equivalent capacity (same GPU type and count) and same model build.
[00:07:36] Ravi Singh: If we fix on A100-80GB for Dedicated and private, is that enough to be comparable?
[00:07:40] Ethan Liu: Yes, but also document driver/OS/kernel versions. Small differences can change kernel choice and perf. We'll include an environment snapshot in every run.
[00:07:52] Naomi Patel: Also include a canary test - a small subset of prompts with high sensitivity to measure accuracy differences when switching quantization or running on different kernels.
[00:08:01] Maya Thompson: Good. For result comparison, how do you recommend we present tradeoffs? A table with p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, cost per 1M tokens, and an accuracy delta?
[00:08:10] Ethan Liu: Exactly. We'll provide CSV outputs and a summary dashboard. Each run will have raw logs, aggregated metrics, environment metadata, and diffs. We'll also produce a short summary doc explaining anomalies.
[00:08:22] Lena Ortiz: About stochastic sampling - temperature, top-p. For deterministic apples-to-apples we should set temperature=0? But that may not reflect production configs where sampling is on.
[00:08:31] Ethan Liu: Two strategies: deterministic baseline (temp=0) to compare raw runtime performance, and sampled baseline to measure production-like behavior. Be explicit in metadata which mode used.
[00:08:43] Naomi Patel: Ok quick note on randomness: record RNG seeds and include reproducible output for deterministic runs.
[00:08:49] Ravi Singh: Regarding quantization: do you offer mixed-precision fallbacks? We want to know if a quantized run falls back to FP16 for certain ops.
[00:09:00] Ethan Liu: We log kernel fallbacks. The runtime emits a kernel-selection log and if an op falls back we flag it in the run metadata. We'll surface those events since they can explain perf anomalies.
[00:09:10] Maya Thompson: Excellent. Edge-case - how do you measure cost? We want cost per useful token or per request.
[00:09:15] Ethan Liu: Cost modeling: tokens-per-GPU-second and infrastructure cost per hour. We'll produce a normalized cost per 1M tokens metric and an estimated monthly cost given your traffic profile.
[00:09:26] Naomi Patel: Also show sensitivity analysis: e.g., if batching increased by X ms, cost drops by Y% but p99 increases by Z ms.
[00:09:33] Lena Ortiz: Will the harness simulate many concurrent users or just concurrent requests? We have long-polling streams from some clients.
[00:09:39] Ethan Liu: The harness supports both short requests and streaming sessions. For streaming we simulate a client that opens a stream, sends incremental input, and measures token emission latency. We can emulate long-lived sessions.
[00:09:50] Ravi Singh: One more: cold-start variance depends on model weight loading times for on-prem. How do you separate disk I/O from runtime cost?
[00:09:58] Ethan Liu: We'll capture disk read times and model-load events in the logs. For on-prem cold starts we can run a separate benchmark that measures model load time in isolation and another that measures steady-state inference.
[00:10:10] Naomi Patel: Ok let's summarize the experiment matrix we'll run for the POC:
[00:10:14] Naomi Patel: 1) Baseline deterministic no-batch runs (hosted, dedicated, private)
[00:10:18] Naomi Patel: 2) Warm vs cold KV cache comparisons
[00:10:21] Naomi Patel: 3) Batching sweep (0ms, 20ms, 50ms, 100ms)
[00:10:25] Naomi Patel: 4) Quantization variants with accuracy diffs (FP16, int8, mixed)
[00:10:30] Ethan Liu: 5) Streaming vs non-streaming tests, measuring first-token and per-token latency
[00:10:34] Ethan Liu: 6) Autoscale locked vs autoscale-enabled runs to show scaling noise
[00:10:38] Ethan Liu: We'll also run a sensitivity analysis for prompt length buckets: short (<=64 tokens), medium (65-256), long (>256).
[00:10:47] Maya Thompson: Timeline for the POC?
[00:10:50] Naomi Patel: Proposed: collect prompts and SLOs by Mon 3/16, share harness by Tue 3/17, Arcadia provisions VPC runner by 3/20, initial runs 3/22-3/24, review 3/26. Adjust as needed.
[00:11:02] Ravi Singh: Works for us. A couple of detail questions: does your harness obfuscate logs before sending back to Redwood storage?
[00:11:09] Ethan Liu: Yes - we support redaction hooks and hashing. If you'd prefer no logs leave VPC and we only ingest aggregated metrics, that's possible.
[00:11:17] Lena Ortiz: Ok we'll probably start with synthetic prompts then move to redacted real prompts.
[00:11:21] Naomi Patel: Anything else? Competitors? Any particular folks you're benchmarking against?
[00:11:25] Maya Thompson: We're also running small comparisons against OpenAI and Anthropic for apples-to-apples latency. But main concern is infra behavior for private deployments.
[00:11:33] Ethan Liu: We'll keep that in mind - ensure license/usage rules for external vendors are followed if you want us to include them.
